speaker: EN_A
text: Welcome to KC Desk Notes. Today we are unpacking one fresh research report and the question it raises.

speaker: EN_A
text: Welcome back to the show. Today we’re digging into a major shift in Fed policy expectations.

speaker: EN_A
text: The latest report from Nomura now sees the Fed on hold indefinitely. EN_B, what’s the big picture here?

speaker: EN_B
text: That’s right. The report’s title, ‘Hawkward Pause, ’ really captures it. The analysts had previously forecast two rate cuts this year,

speaker: EN_B
text: in September and December. Now they expect no cuts at all for the foreseeable future.

speaker: EN_A
text: So what changed their minds? Was it one big thing or a combination of factors?

speaker: EN_B
text: It’s a combination. The report points to three main drivers. First, policy-related pressure for rate cuts has eased. Second, inflation is proving sticky.

speaker: EN_B
text: And third, the economy is still growing strongly. Together, they make a strong case for a prolonged pause.

speaker: EN_A
text: Let’s start with the policy-related side. The report mentions President Trump and incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. How does that play into the call?

speaker: EN_B
text: Interestingly, the report says President Trump has appeared to back off from pushing for rate cuts.

speaker: EN_B
text: He’s quoted in Fortune saying you can’t really look at the figures until the war is over. And he reportedly said he’ll let Warsh do what he wants.

speaker: EN_A
text: So the policy-related heat has diminished.

speaker: EN_A
text: And what about Warsh himself? Wouldn’t he be inclined to cut?

speaker: EN_B
text: The report thinks he likely is still motivated to ease. But the key point is that support among other Fed officials for an easing bias has been waning.

speaker: EN_B
text: Even dovish members are no longer advocating for cuts. So Warsh would need to convince a majority, and that’s looking tough.

speaker: EN_A
text: Let’s talk about the inflation picture. The report mentions some new price pressures. What’s driving that?

speaker: EN_B
text: Tariff inflation has started to fade, but new pressures have emerged. The report specifically cites the Iran war and a global shortage of memory chips.

speaker: EN_B
text: These are pushing up input costs. The S&P Manufacturing PMI input price index surged to 79. 5 in May, the largest monthly increase on record.

speaker: EN_A
text: That’s a big jump. And on the growth side, the economy seems to be holding up well.

speaker: EN_B
text: Exactly. The report highlights robust investment and steady consumption. Manufacturing and business capex are accelerating. Their Q2 GDP tracking is at 2. 6%,

speaker: EN_B
text: and real final sales to private domestic purchasers are at 2. 9%. That’s not an economy that needs stimulus.

speaker: EN_A
text: So with strong growth and sticky inflation, the Fed has little reason to cut. But what about the labor market? Is that also supporting the pause?

speaker: EN_B
text: Yes. The report says labor markets are stabilizing. ADP data shows private payrolls accelerating. And initial jobless claims are sideways,

speaker: EN_B
text: which is actually positive given the seasonal tendency for them to rise into summer. So no signs of weakness there.

speaker: EN_A
text: That all sounds very clear. But is there anything in the report that’s still uncertain? Something that makes the full report worth reading?

speaker: EN_B
text: Definitely. The report doesn’t fully settle what happens if inflation surprises to the upside or if growth suddenly falters.

speaker: EN_B
text: It also leaves open how Warsh’s leadership might evolve. The full report has more detailed data and scenarios. For example,

speaker: EN_A
text: it breaks down the April FOMC minutes and shows how support for easing has shifted.

speaker: EN_A
text: Good point. So for listeners who want the full picture, the report is a must-read. EN_B, any final thought on what this means for the market debate?

speaker: EN_B
text: I’d say this report reinforces the idea that we’re in a new regime. The old playbook of cutting rates at the first sign of trouble may not apply.

speaker: EN_B
text: The Fed is comfortable holding steady, and the data supports that. It’s a fascinating time for monetary policy.

speaker: EN_A
text: Great insights. We’ll leave it there for now. Thanks for walking us through the report. And to our audience,

speaker: EN_A
text: feel free to join the community discussion on the full report. Until next time.
